comment-block.comment: Opens at ## and closes at the NEXT ##, which takes the rest of its line with it. The closer must therefore match to end of line, or a line reading '## and then some' would leave the tail as code. Labels inside are picked out, which is what tells a reader at a glance whether a block is documentation or a remark — the same question the compiler asks of it.
comment-block.name: comment.block.profi-c

documentation-label.comment:
A label inside a documentation comment: the mark, the name and the colon together, but not the prose after it. Matched wherever it appears rather than only above a declaration, since a grammar cannot see what follows a comment and coloring it either way says the same true thing — this line is a label. The mark is required, which is exactly the rule the scanner reads by, so prose wrapping onto a line that begins with a word and a colon is left alone.

Scoped as a language constant rather than a keyword, and the choice is about what a reader sees. An extension cannot set a color: 'configurationDefaults' does not reach editor.tokenColorCustomizations, so whatever scope is chosen here is what the theme paints. Keyword scopes are painted in a theme's loudest color, which is wrong for a line addressed to tooling; constant scopes are painted in a cool one. The names are a fixed set the language defines, so the scope is honest as well as legible.

comment-directive.comment: A line comment the compiler heeds. It stays in the comment family, so a theme that colors all comments still colors this, but the name is its own so it can be set apart — which the extension does by default, since a line addressed to the compiler is not prose and should not read like it. Only a line comment: a block cannot carry a directive, so no block rule matches this. The pattern accepts exactly what the scanner does, so a comment merely beginning with the word is left to the ordinary rule below: 'ignore' first in the comment, then a severity or an identifier, then whitespace or the end of the line. That last part is what keeps 'ignore opinions' prose.
comment-directive.name: comment.line.number-sign.directive.profi-c

comment-line.comment: A single mark. Placed after the block rule so that ## is never read as two of these. Labels are picked out here too, since one line is enough to document something.
comment-line.name: comment.line.number-sign.profi-c

block-string.comment: An opening run of three or more quotes to a run of the same length, holding nothing that is read. The closer is a back-reference to what opened, so a shorter run inside is text. The lookahead makes the closer the last quotes of a run rather than the first, which is where the scanner ends the string when a run is longer than the delimiter. Offered before the ordinary string rule, or the first two quotes would close an empty one and leave the rest as code.
block-string.name: string.quoted.triple.profi-c

interpolation.comment: A hole holds ordinary code, so the whole grammar is offered inside it and a name, a call or a number reads there as it does anywhere. The braces themselves are marked as punctuation rather than as string, which is what tells a reader where the text stops. A format after the colon is not code and is left as part of the string.
interpolation.name: meta.interpolation.profi-c

patterns.comment: Everything from the colon to the closing braces. Matched before the rest so a pattern such as 'yyyy-MM-dd' is not read as subtraction.

fraction.comment: Matched before the plain number rule, or 22|7 reads as two integers around an operator.
fraction.name: constant.numeric.fraction.profi-c

patterns.comment: A base is offered first, or the leading 0 colors as an integer and the rest as a name.
patterns.name: constant.numeric.integer.profi-c

patterns.comment: A real, with or without a point, so long as it carries an exponent.
patterns.name: constant.numeric.real.profi-c

end.comment: A closer names what it closes, so the pair reads as one thing rather than a keyword beside a noun.

declaration.comment: A word and the name after it, wherever that name can only be a type or a function. Each rule captures the word too, and so has to be offered before the plain keyword rules: a keyword matched on its own consumes itself, and the name beside it is then reached with nothing left to say what it is.

patterns.comment: Held apart from 'namespace' below so it can be colored with 'function' and 'let': the words that introduce a thing which then holds something. A model, a structure, and an enumeration hold members; a function holds a body; a let holds a value. A namespace holds none of those — it only says where a name sits.

A namespace's own name is left plain. It names a place rather than a thing, and coloring it as a type made 'Tour.Shapes' read as though Shapes were declared inside a Tour. The whole dotted name is consumed here even though nothing is said about it, so that the qualifier rule below cannot take the first segment and leave the rest — which is what made these render half one color and half another.
And the namespace a using names, for the same reason and by the same means.
What a model extends is a type and can be nothing else.
Without this the name after 'new' is followed by '(' and reads as a function call, which is the one place the grammar said something untrue rather than nothing.
A caught exception names its type before the name it binds.
Both type operators take a type on the right and nothing else.

qualified-type.comment: A type name with wherever it lives written in front of it. Only the last part names the type; the rest says where to look, and a place is not a thing. Reached through 'patterns' on a capture rather than as a rule of its own, so that every rule which already knows it is holding a type hands the whole run over and gets the split for free — and so that a namespace looks the same here as it does after 'namespace' and 'using', which color nothing.

standard-namespace.comment: Standard is the namespace the language owns, not a type inside it. Consumed here, before the provided types and the qualifier rule below, so that neither takes it for one; whatever follows the dot is still colored by whichever of them applies. Named alone among namespaces because it is the only one whose name the language knows — a program's own namespace in this position cannot be told from a type, and is left to the qualifier rule's guess.

typed-name.comment: A type standing in front of the name it describes, with no keyword to announce it: a field, a local, or a parameter. Offered after the primitive and provided types so those keep their own color, and requiring a leading capital, which is convention rather than rule and so is the one thing here that can quietly miss.

patterns.comment: A parameter whose type is a primitive. The type has to be captured here rather than left for the rule that usually colors it: this match begins at the bracket or comma, one character earlier, and the engine takes whichever match starts first — so leaving the word alone would mean consuming it with nothing said about it.

qualifier.comment: A name with a dot after it: the type a shared member is reached through, or the namespace a type is. Told from a value's member by the leading capital, which is convention rather than rule — a local named Total would be colored as though it were a type. That is the cost of having no semantic model, and it is a smaller one than leaving every 'Program.Run()' and 'Circle.Pi' unlit.

patterns.comment: Words that say what something is or how far it reaches. Kept apart from the primitive types below: a reader telling a modifier from a type at a glance is worth more than the two matching.
patterns.name: storage.modifier.profi-c

patterns.comment: The same words, where no name follows: a lambda written 'function(a, b)', and 'let' anywhere.
patterns.name: keyword.declaration.profi-c

patterns.comment: Words that introduce or compose a declaration.
patterns.name: keyword.other.profi-c

patterns.comment: Spelled out rather than punctuated, which is the point of them. The ones that work on bits are here too: 'bitwise' qualifies the 'and' or 'or' after it, and the rest stand alone.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.word.profi-c

type.comment: The primitive types, and the word that writes the type of a function. 'delegate' sits here rather than with the declaring words because that is what it does: it builds a type, as '[]' and '?' do, and never declares anything.
type.name: storage.type.profi-c

reserved-type.comment: Types the language provides. Not keywords, so the scanner reads them as ordinary names; they are listed here because a reader still meets them as part of the language.
reserved-type.name: support.class.profi-c

call.comment: A name with an argument list after it. Matched late, so a keyword is never taken for one.
